strengths: The severe editorial typography, restrained palette and unusually generous space give the bureau a precise, principled voice suited to institutional architecture work.
Project importance is expressed through image scale, placement and pacing rather than a uniform portfolio grid; the 55× difference in project size becomes a genuine compositional idea.
The proposition, evidence, paid-survey process and willingness to advise against proceeding combine into a highly credible commercial narrative.

Photography is exceptionally well matched to the practice position: existing fabric, difficult interiors and material character dominate, while credits and fictional-status disclosures remain visible.
Mobile preserves hierarchy through varied image widths, offsets and deliberate sequencing instead of merely collapsing the desktop grid.

defects.detail: The primary action is absent from the persistent navigation. Visitors persuaded during the opening proposition or an individual project must travel substantially before encountering “Send us a building,” particularly on mobile.
The mobile work page is thoughtfully recomposed, but several long vertical gaps and alternating inset widths make the middle of the portfolio feel slightly episodic rather than continuously paced.

The licensing and fictional-project disclosure is responsible, but on the work-page opening it competes visibly with the commercial introduction and may momentarily foreground the prototype’s artificiality over the bureau’s expertise.

On the home page, the transition from the three selected projects into “All 5 projects” is visually weak and partially stranded across the screenshot break, reducing the authority of that portfolio index transition.

The contact proposition supplies an email address but offers no concise instruction about what the first message should contain beyond an address and photograph; repeating that microcopy beside the email would reduce hesitation.

summary: This is distinctive, disciplined professional work whose scale hierarchy directly answers the hardest portfolio problem and makes the bureau’s point of view memorable. Its principal weakness is commercial wayfinding: the desired action is persuasive when reached, but insufficiently available at earlier moments of conviction.
